## Cards

### 01 · Know your low
Group: **When you’re low** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes Canada calls a blood sugar below 3.9 mmol/L low `1.1`
- Level 1: below 3.9, down to 3.0 `1.2`
- Level 2: below 3.0 `1.3`
- Level 3: a low at any number where you need someone else’s help to treat it `1.4`
- If you use a sensor, Canadian targets for most people aim for less than 4% of the day below 3.9 `1.5`

> **Note** `1.note` — Some Canadian guidance for driving and for school uses 4.0 instead of 3.9. If your team gave you a number, use theirs.

*Sources for this card:* Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Hypoglycemia: low blood sugar in adults (02/24) (Diabetes Canada); Low Blood Sugar - Symptoms and Actions to Take (Diabète Québec); Time in Range (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Blood Glucose Monitoring in Adults and Children with Diabetes: Update 2021 (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Drive Safe with Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Diabetes and Driving (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Low blood sugar: What it is, and what to do (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada))

### 02 · The Rule of 15
Group: **When you’re low** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Take 15 g of fast-acting sugar `2.1`
- Wait 15 minutes, then check your blood sugar again `2.2`
- If it’s still below 3.9, take another 15 g `2.3`
- Once it’s back up, if your next meal is more than an hour away, have a snack with a starch and a protein `2.4`

> **Note** `2.note` — After a low, anyone who drives, teens included, should wait at least 40 minutes, and until their blood sugar is at least 5.0, before driving. More on driving in Everyday Liivving. ✎ *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Hypoglycemia: low blood sugar in adults (02/24) (Diabetes Canada); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetes and Driving (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Low Blood Sugar - Symptoms and Actions to Take (Diabète Québec); Infant botulism (Health Canada)

### 03 · Glucagon: help someone else gives
Group: **When you’re low** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `glucagon` — Baqsimi (4555); notices: `ui.commerce.pharmacistNotice`

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Glucagon is for a low when the person can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Someone else gives it `3.1`
- It comes as a nasal spray or an injection. Your pharmacist can tell you which is available `3.2`
- Call 911, or have someone call. Give glucagon, turn the person on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth `3.3`
- If a low is affecting the person’s thinking or movement but they can still swallow, Diabetes Canada’s sheet says to give 20 g of fast-acting sugar `3.4`
- At school, staff named in the student’s care plan, and trained, give glucagon when the plan includes consent for it `3.5`

> **Note** `3.note` — Ask your pharmacist to show you how your glucagon works, and check its expiry date from time to time. For a child under 4, ask your child’s team which glucagon to keep.

*Sources for this card:* What is glucagon? (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Glucagon: What it is and how to use it (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada)); Hypoglycemia: low blood sugar in adults (02/24) (Diabetes Canada); Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 04 · Lows that sneak up
Group: **When you’re low** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Exercise can keep lowering your blood sugar for up to 48 hours afterwards `4.1`
- Check your blood sugar regularly, especially if you take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar `4.2`
- If you take insulin or some diabetes pills, alcohol can cause a low up to 24 hours after you drink `4.3`
- Diabetes Canada suggests eating carbohydrate when you drink, and checking your blood sugar before bed `4.4`
- Make sure someone with you knows to call 911 if you pass out, and to give you glucagon if you have it. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says glucagon may not work as well if you’ve had more than 2 standard drinks in the past few hours, so the 911 call matters even more ✎ `4.5`
- A sensor can run up to 15 minutes behind your blood sugar. Diabetes Canada suggests keeping a meter as a backup `4.6`

> **Note** `4.note` — Ask your team how to plan your medicines around exercise and drinking.

*Sources for this card:* Exercise & Activity (Diabetes Canada); Alcohol and diabetes (04/18) (Diabetes Canada); Nutrition Therapy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetes and Drinking (Diabetes Canada); Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 05 · Carry it, wear it
Group: **When you’re low** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `carry` — Dex4 Fast Acting Glucose Tablets Tropical Fruit (7371), Dex4 Glucose Gel Fruit Punch (7382), Dex4 Key Chain (4731), PharmaSystems Med ID Bracelet Diabetic (7778), 2BEID Medical Alert Bracelets Small (4289)

- Carry fast-acting sugar when you’re active `5.1`
- If you have glucagon, show the people you spend time with how it works. Diabetes Canada’s guideline says they should be taught `5.2`
- Wear medical ID, such as a bracelet or necklace `5.3`
- For a child at school, a care plan made before the school year covers daily care and emergencies, with at least two trained staff `5.4`
- Diabetes@School says to treat a student’s low right away, where it happens, and not to leave them alone `5.5`
- Students may carry a phone or smartwatch to help manage their blood sugar `5.6`

*Sources for this card:* Exercise & Activity (Diabetes Canada); Alcohol and diabetes (04/18) (Diabetes Canada); Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Managing type 1 diabetes in school (CPS position statement, 2015) (Canadian Paediatric Society); Kids with Diabetes in School (Diabetes Canada); Low blood sugar: What it is, and what to do (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada))

### 06 · Highs
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Diabetes Canada’s usual targets are 4.0 to 7.0 mmol/L before meals and 5.0 to 10.0 two hours after meals. Your team may set different ones `6.1`
- Symptoms of a high can show up when your fasting blood sugar is 11 or higher `6.2`
- If your blood sugar stays above 14 before meals for more than a few meals, check for ketones `6.3`
- Ketones can build up even when blood sugar is close to normal, for example in pregnancy or with a type of diabetes pill called an SGLT2 inhibitor. Ask your pharmacist whether any of your pills is, or contains, one ✎ `6.4`

> **Note** `6.note` — Very high blood sugar or high ketones need care right away. The signs are at the top of this page.

*Sources for this card:* Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada); Hyperglycemia (Diabetes Canada); Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada)

### 07 · Ketones: check and act
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Ketones build up when your body doesn’t have enough insulin and starts breaking down fat for energy `7.1`
- You can check ketones in your blood or in your urine. Your team will tell you which to use `7.2`
- Check when your blood sugar stays high. With type 1, check when you’re sick too, especially with vomiting, stomach pain or a fever. With other types, check when you’re sick if your team has told you to `7.3`
- Diabetes Canada’s guideline for type 1 diabetes says to put off hard exercise if blood ketones are 1.5 or higher `7.4`
- Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) include thirst, passing a lot of urine, stomach pain, feeling or being sick, deeper breathing, fruity-smelling breath, and feeling tired, sleepy or confused. DKA needs medical care right away `7.5`

> **Note** `7.note` — The ladder below is adapted from Breakthrough T1D and was written for type 1 diabetes. If you have another type, ask your team which numbers to use. With any type, Diabetes Canada says high ketones need medical care right away. ✎

*Sources for this card:* Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Hyperglycemia (Diabetes Canada); Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada); Physical Activity and Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 08 · Sick days
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

**When it applies** `8.s1`

- Diabetes Canada’s sick-day sheet is for vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or a lot of heat or humidity without enough to drink: anything that can leave you dehydrated `8.s1.1`

**What the sheet says to do** `8.s2`

- Drink plenty of fluids with little sugar, unless you’ve been told to limit fluids `8.s2.1`
- If you can’t eat, the sheet lists foods with 15 g of carbohydrate to have instead `8.s2.2`
- Diabetes Canada says that if you use insulin, you should keep taking it when you’re sick. Check your blood sugar more often. The sheet says your insulin may need adjusting, so ask your team how ✎ `8.s2.3`

**Your medicines on sick days** `8.s3`

- The sheet lists some medicines to stop for a short time if you’re eating less, or dehydrated, for more than 24 hours `8.s3.1`
- Which of your own medicines this means is a question for your pharmacist. The sheet has a space for them to write it down `8.s3.2`
- The sheet says to restart them once you’re eating and drinking normally `8.s3.3`

**When to call** `8.s4`

- Vomiting and can’t keep fluids down: go to the emergency department. If you can reach your team right away, call them too `8.s4.1`
- If you’re sick and can’t eat, call your doctor or go to the emergency department if you vomit or have diarrhea 2 or more times in 4 hours ✎ `8.s4.2`
- Call your team or go to the emergency department if you can’t drink enough, don’t know which medicines to stop or how to adjust your insulin, or your ketones are moderate. Large ketones need emergency care now ✎ `8.s4.3`
- Do the same if vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, passing a lot of urine, extreme thirst, weakness or fever isn’t getting better. Trouble breathing needs emergency care now `8.s4.4`

> **Note** `8.note` — Fill in the plan on this card with your pharmacist and diabetes team before you’re sick, so it’s ready when you need it. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Checking Blood Sugar (Diabetes Canada)

### 09 · On a pump: an unexplained high
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes Canada suggests keeping backup supplies, such as rapid-acting insulin pens or syringes, and learning how to switch to injections in case you can’t use your pump `9.1`
- If your blood sugar is high and you can’t explain it, check your ketones and follow the ladder in Ketones: check and act `9.2`
- Keep a written copy of your pump settings in your emergency kit `9.3`

> **Note** `9.note` — Your pump team’s plan comes first. Ask them what to do if you think your pump has stopped giving insulin.

*Sources for this card:* Technology & Devices (Diabetes Canada); Managing Diabetes in Emergency Situations (Diabetes Canada); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF))

### 10 · Be ready for emergencies
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask a pharmacist** · Products shown: *none*

- Diabetes Canada suggests an emergency kit with at least one to two weeks of supplies `10.1`
- Include fast-acting sugar, glucagon if you have it, ketone strips and a sharps container `10.2`
- If you use a pump, add a written copy of your settings `10.3`
- Diabète Québec says to keep unopened insulin in the fridge, at 2 to 8 °C. Throw out insulin that has frozen, been above 30 °C, or expired `10.4`
- How long an opened pen or vial lasts depends on the product. Diabète Québec says most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer. Follow the leaflet that came with your insulin ✎ `10.5`

*Sources for this card:* Managing Diabetes in Emergency Situations (Diabetes Canada); All about injections (Diabète Québec); Getting Started with Insulin (Diabetes Canada)

### 11 · Who to call, and when
Group: **When you’re high, or sick** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- 911: someone can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure `11.1`
- Emergency department, or 911: blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA such as deep breathing or fruity-smelling breath `11.2`
- Your diabetes team, now: blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones. If you can’t reach them, go to the emergency department ✎ `11.3`
- Your diabetes team: blood ketones 0.6 to under 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones ✎ `11.4`
- Your pharmacist: your sick-day medicine plan, and how your glucagon works `11.5`

## Emergency red flags

*Pinned open, and never behind a French review gate.*

**Get emergency care now** `urgent.heading`

Everyday lows and highs follow your plan. These don’t. Get emergency care now if the person: `urgent.intro`

1. Can’t swallow, is unconscious or is having a seizure. Call 911, give glucagon if you have it, turn them on their side and stay with them. Don’t put food or drink in their mouth `urgent.1`
2. Is vomiting and can’t keep fluids down `urgent.2`
3. Has blood ketones above 3.0 mmol/L, or large ketones in their urine (ranges written for type 1 diabetes) `urgent.3`
4. Has deep or hard breathing or fruity-smelling breath, or is very sleepy or confused with a high blood sugar or ketones. In pregnancy, or with some diabetes medicines, DKA can happen even when blood sugar is near normal ✎ `urgent.4`

**Action** `urgent.action` — Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

## Referral band

*Sources for the band:* Chapter 14: 2023 Update – Hypoglycemia in Adults (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and ketones (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Stay Safe When You Have Diabetes and Are Sick or at Risk of Dehydration (Diabetes Canada); What is glucagon? (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Glucagon: What it is and how to use it (Diabetes@School (Canadian Paediatric Society, CPEG and Diabetes Canada))

**The safety ladder** `band.heading`

- **Treat and check again** `band.1` — A low: take 15 g of fast-acting sugar, wait 15 minutes and check again. Still below 3.9? Take 15 g more. For a child, the amount depends on their age: see The Rule of 15.
  - *Where card 2's title appears in this body, it links to card 2.*
- **Call your team** `band.2` — Blood ketones 0.6 to under 1.5 when you’re sick, or small urine ketones. ✎
- **Call your team now** `band.3` — Blood ketones 1.5 to 3.0, or moderate urine ketones. If you can’t reach your team, go to the emergency department. ✎
- **Emergency care, or 911** `band.4` — Can’t swallow, unconscious or having a seizure: call 911. Blood ketones over 3.0, large urine ketones, vomiting with no fluids kept down, or signs of DKA: get emergency care now.

## Closing

**A plan you already know** `closing.heading`

Staying safe is the same few steps, practised: check, act, check again, and know when to call. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for care from your diabetes team, doctor or pharmacist. Your targets, your medicines and your sick-day plan depend on you. Your team sets them. `disclaimer`

(2020) and is « Adapté de » a FIT PDF hosted by embecta (fit4diabetes.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/EMB-25-441-FIT-Recommendations-Update-Layout_F00-1.pdf); it gives in-use times of 28 days (42 for detemir and Toujeo, 56 for degludec), says a skin fold is « recommandé si on utilise une aiguille de 8 mm », and to avoid injecting within 2 to 3 cm of the navel. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C14): Diabète Québec is a Canadian non-industry patient organization that publishes and reviews these lines under its own name, so they stay live beside Diabetes Canada’s; lines whose only source is FIT stay held. Ruled 2026-10-06 (C15): "most are good for up to 28 days once opened, and some for longer" is cited to this page (Your Tools card 11, Staying Safe card 10). Reviewer evidence on in-use times from the Health Canada monographs (C7): Toujeo 42 days, Humalog 28, Tresiba 56, Awiqli 12 weeks, Entuzity 28. | <https://www.diabete.qc.ca/en/diabetes/diabetes-management/insulin/all-about-injections/> |

The time-in-range targets are the International Consensus Report’s, adopted here, and they exclude pregnancy, children and adolescents, and older or high-risk groups. Link this 2021 update, never the older chapter 9. | <https://www.diabetes.ca/for-professionals/full-guidelines/chapter-9-2021-update> |
